# Bar fridges and spite

Jonno,

You’ve messaged me about the coolroom three times now, so here you go. A written record. This is the sort of service you get when you’re one of about 40 people reading this thing and the other main reader is my mum.

You would’ve lost your fucking mind.

Actually, old Jonno would’ve lost his mind, then got on with it. London Jonno, who’s been gone since February and is presumably wearing a coat with buttons, would’ve needed a little sit-down.

Anyway. Cup Day.

Tuesday, 3 November. I get in at 6.40am and the coolroom thermometer says 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Lovely temperature for a walk. Less good for a room whose entire job is being cold.

Compressor had died overnight. Just quietly clocked off between Monday and Tuesday, leaving us with 140 booked for lunch. Set menu. Three courses. Raff was away, so I was running it, which was an exciting opportunity to develop professionally by staring at a thermometer and saying “fuck” to nobody.

You know that first bit where you look again because maybe you’ve read it wrong? As if the thermometer’s going to go, sorry mate, upside down, all good.

Still 11.

Called Wally from Coldline. Couldn’t get there till Wednesday. Part coming from Sydney.

I don’t blame Wally. Wally cannot personally make Sydney closer. But hearing “Wednesday” at that particular moment did make me want to put my phone in the bin.

Phil’s contribution was “just make it work mate”.

Cheers Phil. Hadn’t considered that. I was going to stand out the front and wave people away with a tea towel, but now you’ve explained the strategy we’ll get cracking.

“Just make it work” is not a plan. It’s what you say when you’d like someone else to have one.

So we found fridge space.

Both undercounters. The bar fridge. Half of Marta’s walk-in next door, because Marta is a better person than any of us and should probably own the bistro. Anything we could safely keep went wherever there was room. Everything else was a loss.

About $1,800 of stock gone, mostly dairy and the duck legs.

I’ll give you a moment for the duck legs. I know you’d have taken that personally.

The kitchen was now spread across two businesses, and getting something out of the fridge had become a trip. You know how you used to crack the shits if someone put your stuff one shelf away from where you wanted it? Imagine me telling you it was next door.

You’d have been unbearable.

The beef shin was the best bit. Thirty kilos of it, me and Benny, down the laneway in the rain on a milk crate trolley.

Then a wheel fell off.

Of course a wheel fell off. It would’ve been disappointing, structurally, if the trolley had simply worked.

There’s not much dignity available when you’re trying to get 30 kilos of beef through a wet laneway, but we’d apparently been holding on to some, because the wheel sorted that out.

I thought of you then. Genuinely. Not because I missed you. Because you would’ve had a lot to say about how we were doing it, and I was glad you were in England.

Kev, meanwhile, was on ice. Not like that, Mum, if you’re reading.

He filled the old esky with 14 bags from the servo. Fourteen bags. Servo bloke asked if we were having a party.

Yes mate. Big one. Starts at lunch, 140 coming, none of them know the fridge is dead. Kev’s doing ice, I’m doing a quiet nervous breakdown, and there’s beef arriving via a transport system Benny and I can no longer recommend.

By this point the bar fridge was doing work well outside its position description. You spend years treating it like the stupid little fridge and then suddenly it’s essential infrastructure.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. I’m putting that in writing so you can’t steal it.

And somehow, lunch happened.

Not “somehow” as in magic. Everyone just got properly stuck in. There wasn’t room for anyone to be precious, which is another reason it was good you weren’t there.

Honestly, best service we did all year.

I know how that sounds after the beef trolley, but it was. Everyone was locked in. Benny, Kev, everyone. We’d spent the morning moving things, binning things, finding space and working out what we could actually serve, and then we had to serve it.

So we did.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

That’s not me being coy about some clever replacement dessert. It was affogato with whatever. Three-course set menu, very professional operation, please direct any questions to Phil’s detailed business plan.

People loved it.

Possibly more than they would’ve loved the panna cotta, which I’m trying not to think about. There’s something deeply annoying about having a dessert planned, losing it, throwing together the alternative and getting a response that suggests you should’ve just done that in the first place.

Fine. Next menu is all whatever. Whatever entrée, beef from outside, whatever dessert. Bookings essential.

The lady on table nine had seen me and Benny out the window. Asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

Fair play.

Absolutely nothing I can say to that. She’d watched the supply chain. She was entitled to ask.

I’m glad you weren’t there for that either, actually. You’d still be saying it in March. Every time beef came up. Every time a trolley came up. Every time anyone looked out a window.

Marta, being no fool, has arranged repayment in croissant credit. I reckon I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. Fair enough. Half a walk-in on Cup Day isn’t a small favour, and she could’ve asked for considerably worse.

Please don’t message her suggesting a rate. You live overseas now. Stay out of local affairs.

Oh, and my horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad.

Came second last.

I’d like to make it clear I did not arrange that name for the purposes of this post. That was genuinely the horse I got on the day the coolroom died. Apparently losing $1,800 worth of stock wasn’t enough. The universe wanted a little joke as well.

So that’s what happened with the coolroom.

It was shit at 6.40am. It was still pretty shit when the wheel came off. It’s funny now, and I’m allowed to be pleased with the service without pretending I’d like to do any of it again.

You would’ve been good to have on grill. I’ll give you that much, since you’re so far away you can’t immediately become a pain in the arse about it.

But you’d have cried. London’s made you soft. One wet laneway and you’d have been asking what the procedure was.

Come home ya flog.
